title: Hybrid TTL+LRU eviction validator and KV lease coordinator for GPU-resident caches
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: GPU-resident KV cache entries are being evicted under memory pressure in ways that can break correctness for continuous-batching inference workloads. Batches often reference the same prefixes across concurrent requests; naive TTL or LRU evictions race with in-flight KV reuse leading to stale keys, double-free-like memory corruption, or silent correctness regressions in model outputs.

Goal: Design and validate a hybrid eviction scheme combining TTL, LRU, and prefix-aware lease coordination that: 1) prevents invalid read-after-evict for in-flight batches, 2) bounds GPU memory footprint and fragmentation, and 3) provides clear correctness invariants that can be proven/tested and rolled out safely with telemetry and canary gating.

Scope: Implement a KV lease coordinator and validator harness in the runtime, plus unit/property tests, mem-pressure simulations, and chaos tests in staging. Do not change public API. Work includes runtime changes (cache metadata, atomic generation ids), eviction policy adjustments, and observability (eviction telemetry and invariants).

Key ideas and invariants: 
- Lease tokens: Each cache allocation is stamped with an epoch (generation id) and a short-lived lease token when returned to the caller for potential reuse by batched requests. Inflight consumers hold the lease token; only when the lease is explicitly released (or expires) may eviction repurpose memory.
- Atomic generation id: Cache entries carry a monotonically-increasing generation integer; readers validate that the generation matches the lease token before using the KV pointer. Any mismatch causes immediate safe-fallback to recompute the prefix or fall back to CPU path. This prevents use-after-evict races.
- Hybrid TTL+LRU policy: We maintain two ordered lists: a TTL-ordered wheel for coarse timeouts (helps long-lived prefixes) and an age-ordered LRU list for capacity pressure. Eviction candidates are selected by score = alpha * normalized_age + beta * normalized_ttl_expiry, tunable per-deployment. Prefix-awareness: prefixes marked as hot (per prefix counters) are scored lower to avoid removing short-lived prompt prefixes mid-batch.
- Lease-aware eviction: Evictor respects active lease tokens: entries with active leases are only evicted after lease expiration or forced reclamation via coordinated preemption (see preemption below). Forced preemption is a last-resort path that increments the global epoch and invalidates all matching leases atomically, forcing in-flight requests to detect eviction and re-fetch safely.
- Preemption and epoch semantics: To avoid long blocking under extreme memory pressure, we support an epoch bump preemption API: the evictor can increment the global epoch for a shard, install a tombstone, and asynchronously compact memory. In-flight holders detect epoch mismatch and either retry (preferred) or abort with a retriable error. This makes invalidation observable and bounded.
- Memory management: Use a slab allocator with size classes to reduce fragmentation on GPU; implement background compaction triggers once free slab fragmentation crosses threshold. Eviction accounting also tracks backpressure from CUDA OOM signals and triggers conservative eviction (increase alpha weight on age) under repeated OOMs.

Correctness guarantees (informal):
1) No use-after-free: Any consumer that reads a KV pointer must validate the generation id against its lease token; mismatch routes to a safe retrieval path.
2) Read-after-evict determinism: Preemption increments epoch deterministically and emits telemetry; clients either observe old epoch and retry or see the new epoch and recompile. There is a bounded window (lease duration + scheduling jitter) in which an in-flight request may fall back but cannot read garbage.
3) Monotonic memory accounting: Evictions and allocations update shard-level counters atomically (compare-and-swap) to prevent double-counting races.

Validation plan: 
- Unit tests: generation id checks, lease renewals, eviction candidate scoring.
- Property tests: fuzz the order/latency of lease release, epoch bumps, and eviction under randomized continuous-batching scenarios; assert invariants (no pointer used after generation mismatch).
- Mem-pressure harness: synthetic driver that triggers CUDA OOM and varying allocation patterns (many small prefixes vs few large prefixes) to exercise fragmentation and compaction paths.
- Integration chaos: run staging with synthetic traffic replay of production traces at 1x-5x with tail latency collectors, metric assertions, and automatic rollback on correctness regression signals.
- Benchmark: throughput and p99 latency before/after with hot prefix skew to ensure hybrid policy does not regress critical paths.

Rollout and telemetry: 
- Start in internal dev staging with evictor disabled by default and run validator harness.
- Canary on 3 Dedicated clusters with lease enforcement turned on and conservative TTL/LRU weights. Collect metrics: lease_contention_rate, epoch_bumps_per_min, eviction_retries_per_request, pointer_mismatch_count, gpu_fragmentation_ratio.
- Gate to broader rollout if pointer_mismatch_count remains zero and epoch_bump-induced retries < 0.1% of requests for 72h.

Acceptance criteria: 
- All unit/property tests green, and chaos runs produce zero silent pointer-use violations.
- End-to-end p99 latency regression <= 5% on canary traffic; throughput loss <= 2% at steady state.
- Telemetry shows stable eviction_retries_per_request and low lease_contention_rate.

Out-of-scope: changes to public API surface, model-level cache warming heuristics (separate RFC), and cross-shard multi-tenant lease sharing (future work).
